exercises.prompt:
A project has two files, `main.cpp` and `stats.cpp`. You build with `g++ -std=c++23 main.cpp -o app` and get:

```text
undefined reference to `mean(std::vector<double, std::allocator<double> > const&)'
```

Which step failed, and what is the most likely cause?

options.label: The linker: `mean` was declared (so `main.cpp` compiled) but its definition, in `stats.cpp`, was never compiled into the program.
options.feedback: Yes. "Undefined reference" is the linker's message. The command only names `main.cpp`; adding `stats.cpp` to it lets the linker find the definition.

options.label: The preprocessor: the header that declares `mean` could not be found.
options.feedback: Not yet — a missing header produces a "No such file or directory" error from the preprocessor before any compiling happens.

options.label: The compiler: `mean` has a type error.
options.feedback: Not yet — compiler errors name a file, line and column inside your source. This message names no line at all, which is a hint that it comes from a later step.

options.label: The running program: it crashed while calling `mean`.
options.feedback: Not yet — with this error no executable is produced, so nothing ran.

hints: Which tool's job is it to connect a call in one file to a definition in another?
Look at which files the command line actually names.
exercises.solution: The message *undefined reference* comes from the **linker**. `main.cpp` compiled because it saw a *declaration* of `mean` (probably from a header), which is all the compiler needs to check a call. But the *definition* lives in `stats.cpp`, which was never compiled, so when the linker joined the pieces nothing provided `mean`. The fix is `g++ -std=c++23 main.cpp stats.cpp -o app`, or, in a real project, a build system that knows the list of files.

hints: `>5` right-aligns in five columns, `<3` left-aligns in three, `^7` centres in seven.
`42` needs three spaces in front of it to fill five columns.
exercises.solution: It prints `[   42|7  |  mid  ]`. `{:>5}` puts `42` at the right of a 5-wide field (three spaces, then `42`); `{:<3}` puts `7` at the left of a 3-wide field (`7` and two spaces); `{:^7}` centres the 3-letter `mid` in 7 columns, leaving two spaces on each side.

feedback.message: Not yet — when both operands of `/` are integers, C++ performs integer division and throws away the fractional part.

hints: What are the types of `7` and `2`? Of `7.0`?
`%` is the remainder after integer division.
exercises.solution: It prints `3 1 3.5`. `7 / 2` divides two `int`s, so the result is an `int` and the fraction is discarded: `3`. `7 % 2` is the remainder, `1`. In `7.0 / 2` one operand is a `double`, so the other is converted and the division is done in floating point: `3.5`. This is the same rule as in C and Java, and differs from Python 3, where `/` always gives a float.

feedback.message: Not yet — check the value of `i` after the third step: is it still less than 20?
Not yet — the step is `i *= 3` (multiply by three), not `i += 3`.

hints: Write down the values `i` takes: it starts at 1 and is multiplied by 3 after each pass.
The loop stops as soon as `i < 20` is false.
exercises.solution: `i` takes the values 1, 3 and 9, and the body runs once for each, so `count` becomes 3. The next value, 27, fails `i < 20` and the loop ends. The program prints **3**.

hints: `push_back` adds an element at the end.
The comparison is strictly greater, so a later name of the same length does not replace an earlier one.
exercises.solution: It prints `4 Mateus`. After `push_back` the vector holds four names. `longest` starts empty; the loop replaces it with `Ngozi` (5 letters), keeps it for `Aiko` (4), replaces it with `Mateus` (6), and keeps it for `Leila` (5). The `const auto&` in the loop visits each string without copying it, an idiom you will see in every lesson.

exercises.prompt: Which of these follow from C++'s **zero-overhead principle**? Select all that apply.

options.label: A program that never throws an exception should not pay for exceptions on its normal path.
options.feedback: Yes. Mainstream implementations make the non-throwing path cost (almost) nothing; the cost is paid only when something is thrown.

options.label: There is no garbage collector running in the background of every program.
options.feedback: Yes. A collector would cost every program time and memory, including programs that manage memory in other ways.

options.label: Every array access is checked against the array's bounds, because safety has no cost.
options.feedback: Not yet — a check on every access does cost something, which is exactly why plain indexing in C++ is unchecked. (Hardened library modes and `.at()` let you choose checks when you want them.)

options.label: Using `std::sort` should be no slower than a sort you would write by hand for the same type.
options.feedback: Yes. Templates let the library generate code specialised for your type and comparison, so the abstraction does not cost speed.

hints: The principle has two halves: what you do not use, and what you do use.
Does the language add any cost to programs that do not ask for it?
exercises.solution: The principle says that features you do not use cost nothing, and features you do use cost no more than hand-written code. (a), (b) and (d) follow. (c) does not: bounds-checking every access would impose a cost on every program, so C++ makes unchecked `v[i]` the default and offers checked access (`v.at(i)`, or a hardened standard library mode) when you choose it. Whether that default is still the right one is one of the live debates around C++ today.

exercises.prompt: In which year did C++ first become an ISO international standard?

feedback.message: Not yet — 1985 is the first commercial release and the first edition of Stroustrup's book. Standardisation came later.
Not yet — C++11 was the big modernisation, but it revised an existing standard.

hints: The first standard is often called by a two-digit name, like the later C++11 and C++20.
exercises.solution: **1998**: ISO/IEC 14882:1998, usually called C++98. It was lightly corrected in 2003 (C++03), substantially modernised in 2011, and has been revised every three years since.
